title: Will the Midterms Hurt J.D. Vance’s Presidential Chances in 2028?
author: Chantelle Lee
body:
Democrats’ sweeping wins in the midterm elections have dealt a devastating blow to President Donald Trump, and could spell trouble for the speculated presidential ambitions of his second-in-command, Vice President J.D. Vance, as the contest to succeed Trump on the Republican ticket and in the Oval Office looms.

Vance is widely considered to be one of the top potential Republican contenders for the 2028 presidential election, though he has previously dismissed suggestions that he intends to run for the White House in two years. (Vance’s office did not respond to a request for comment on this article.)

Still, many people have predicted that Vance will ultimately throw his hat in the ring, along with other notable GOP names, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told POLITICO last week that he is “not going to take sides because we’ll have, probably, several senators maybe in that conversation." Trump himself, meanwhile, has repeatedly floated a ticket including both Vance and Rubio, without specifying which of the two he would like to run for President or Vice President.

Vance led a group of potential candidates for the Republican presidential nomination in a recent YouGov/Economist survey conducted in the wake of the midterm elections, with 40% of respondents saying that they would be most likely to vote for the Vice President to get the GOP nod if the primary were held today.

But many political pundits have read the results of this month’s elections as a stunning rebuke of Trump—one that, they say, could throw a wrench into a potential Vance presidential run in 2028.

“The midterms were viewed as being a rebuff of the Administration, which went beyond even the normal loss that the presidential party suffers in the initial midterm,” says Joel K. Goldstein, an expert on the Vice Presidency who has written two books on the subject. “This was much more sweeping and dramatic.”

Read More: Are Democrats’ Stunning Midterm Upsets in Deep-Red States a Blip—or Is Their Map Expanding?

Much of Democrats’ success in the midterms has been attributed to the unpopularity of the President, whose approval rating in the month leading up to Election Day dropped to a historic low, due in large part to the public’s disapproval over his approach to the economy and the Iran war.

And because Vance is “closely tied to the Trump Administration,” he “ends up being tarnished” in the aftermath of the midterms, Goldstein says.

“Before the midterms, J.D. Vance kind of had [the Republican nomination] almost locked down,” says GOP consultant Barrett Marson. “Now, there are serious questions about whether he—or anyone in the Administration, quite frankly—would be right.”

The Vice Presidency: A ‘presidential springboard’ with ‘baggage’

Goldstein describes the Vice Presidency as “the best presidential springboard” because it can “elevate” a politician in the national spotlight.

“Nobody was suggesting that Senator Vance run for President in 2024,” Goldstein says. “The fact that he was selected as Trump’s running mate and then was elected sort of catapulted him to prominence and really put him in a strong position on the Republican side and that follows sort of a normal pattern of Vice Presidents.”

On the other hand, Goldstein points out that there are disadvantages to the job—a major one being that the Vice President ends up inheriting “the baggage” of the Administration. Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, says former Vice President Kamala Harris was in a similar position when she ran for President in 2024.

“Part of what made it so difficult for Kamala Harris in 2024 was the high level of dissatisfaction with Joe Biden and perceptions about how his policies or lack thereof affected inflation and prices across the country,” Panagopoulos says. “It’s not only difficult for Vice Presidents to get out of the shadow of the President whose Administration they served and establish themselves as an independent voice—it’s even harder when those Presidents are unpopular.”

“[Harris] was stuck between a rock and a hard place, and J.D. Vance is going to find himself in the same position,” he continues. “I think the same could be said for several high-profile Republicans who are serving in or who have served in the Trump Administration—but there’s no individual who is as closely linked to a President as the Vice President.”

What could Vance do to mitigate fallout from the midterms?

Political experts agree that one strategy Vance could take in the aftermath of the midterms is to try to “distance” himself from the President.

The public saw a first glimpse of that the morning after Election Day: In a lengthy social media post, Vance blamed the Republican losses in the midterms on the unpopularity of the Iran war.

“There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that's true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone,” Vance said. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.”

News outlets have reported that Vance had shared reservations in private about launching the war in the Middle East.

When asked about Vance’s social media post, Trump told reporters that he thought the message was “largely true because [the war] drove the gasoline up a little.” But he said, again, that he stood by his decision to launch the war.

“At the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again because long-term, it’s the only answer,” Trump said.

Political experts cast doubt that Vance’s post would be enough to distance himself, in the public’s view, from the unpopular conflict. Marson describes Vance’s statement as “incredibly gentle pushback,” adding that the Vice President would “need a course correction—not a tinkering around the edges.”

“He would have to distance himself quite a bit from Trump, and it’s clear that he is trying to do that in part by reinforcing his initial opposition to the war in Iran,” Panagopoulos says. “But that’s going to be a tough sell for the American public because on most other things, he’s backed up the President, and even on things they might have disagreed on, Vance is viewed as a loyal foot soldier for Donald Trump, for MAGA, and for the Republican Party as it is currently constituted.”

The other challenge Vance is facing is that he is currently serving in the Administration. Somebody like Joe Biden, who ran for President in the 2020 election, about three years after he finished his term as Vice President under the Obama Administration, may have a bit of an easier time separating themselves from the Administration they served under since more time has passed, Goldstein says. But people like Vance and Harris may find it more difficult, he says, to distance themselves from the Administration that they are currently working in.

While Trump appears to have been receptive to Vance’s social media post, political experts say that they don’t believe the President will appreciate or welcome his second-in-command publicly criticizing his policies.

“President Trump does not suffer criticism in a gentlemanly manner,” Marson says. “I don’t know that it is possible for any of his direct employees to say one cross word about him and his policies.”

Panagopoulos says that another approach Vance could try is to support or enact policies that “have a tangible positive impact” on issues that Americans are concerned about, particularly affordability and gas prices.

“To the extent that Republicans can deliver on those things and start to rehabilitate the party’s image, that could help Vance,” Panagopoulos says. “Otherwise, anyone with such a close connection to Donald Trump is going to be fighting an uphill battle for 2028. That doesn’t mean that their credentials are still not solid enough within the Republican base to do well in a primary, but once you look ahead to a general election and electability, things could start to look very different for anyone so closely tied to Trump.”
